Information-Theoretic Limits of Safety Verification
for Self-Improving Systems

Arsenios Scrivens
March 2026
Abstract

Can a safety gate permit unbounded beneficial self-modification while maintaining bounded cumulative risk? We formalize this question through dual conditions — requiring ∑δn<∞\sum\delta_{n}<\infty (bounded risk) and ∑TPRn=∞\sum\mathrm{TPR}_{n}=\infty (unbounded utility) — and establish a theory of their (in)compatibility.

Classification impossibility (Theorem 1): For power-law risk schedules δn=O⁡(n−p)\delta_{n}=O(n^{-p}) with p>1p>1 — the practically relevant regime — any classifier-based gate under overlapping safe/unsafe distributions satisfies TPRn≤Cα⋅δnβ\mathrm{TPR}_{n}\leq C_{\alpha}\cdot\delta_{n}^{\beta} via Hölder’s inequality, forcing ∑TPRn<∞\sum\mathrm{TPR}_{n}<\infty. This impossibility is exponent-optimal: no valid impossibility bound can use a larger exponent than β∗\beta^{*} (Theorem 3; full Mills’ ratio asymptotics in Appendix A.3). A second independent proof via the NP counting method (Theorem 4) yields a 13% tighter bound without Hölder’s inequality. Scope caveat: for slowly-decaying summable sequences such as δn=1/(n​ln2​n)\delta_{n}=1/(n\ln^{2}n) that are not power-law, the Hölder summability argument fails and the NP-optimal classifier may satisfy both dual conditions (§3.1). Theorem 5 covers all schedules.

Universal finite-horizon ceiling (Theorem 5): For any summable risk schedule, the exact maximum achievable classifier utility is U∗​(N,B)=N⋅TPRNP​(B/N)U^{*}(N,B)=N\cdot\mathrm{TPR}_{\mathrm{NP}}(B/N), growing as exp⁡(O⁡(log⁡N))\exp(O(\sqrt{\log N})) — subpolynomial. At N=106N=10^{6} with budget B=1.0B=1.0, a classifier extracts at most U∗≈87U^{*}\approx 87 versus a verifier’s ≈500,000\approx 500{,}000. This result is universal: it applies even where Theorem 1 does not.

Verification escape (Theorem 2): A Lipschitz ball verifier achieves δ=0\delta=0 with TPR>0\mathrm{TPR}>0, escaping the impossibility. Formal Lipschitz bounds for pre-LayerNorm transformers under LoRA (Proposition 3) enable LLM-scale verification. The separation is strict: classifiers cannot achieve δ=0\delta=0 with TPR>0\mathrm{TPR}>0 under distribution overlap (Proposition 4). We validate on GPT-2 (dLoRA=147,456d_{\text{LoRA}}=147{,}456): conditional δ=0\delta=0 with TPR=0.352\mathrm{TPR}=0.352; unconditional δ=0\delta=0 at d≤17,408d\leq 17{,}408. Comprehensive empirical validation is in the companion paper [23].

1 Introduction

The prospect of AI systems that improve their own capabilities raises a central safety question: can we build a gate that permits beneficial self-modifications while reliably blocking dangerous ones? We formalize this as a sequential decision problem and provide a comprehensive theoretical characterization of when safe self-improvement is possible and when it is provably impossible.

At each step nn, a system proposes a mutation θn\theta_{n} to its own parameters. A safety gate gng_{n} decides whether to accept or reject θn\theta_{n}, incurring false acceptance rate δn=P−​(gn​ accepts)\delta_{n}=P^{-}(g_{n}\text{ accepts}) and true positive rate TPRn=P+​(gn​ accepts)\mathrm{TPR}_{n}=P^{+}(g_{n}\text{ accepts}). We require ∑δn<∞\sum\delta_{n}<\infty (bounded risk, ensuring positive probability of never accepting an unsafe mutation) and ∑TPRn=∞\sum\mathrm{TPR}_{n}=\infty (unbounded utility, ensuring the system accepts infinitely many improvements). We call these the dual conditions for safe self-improvement.

We prove four impossibility and tightness results and four constructive results, forming a complete picture. The impossibility is strongest for power-law risk schedules δn=O⁡(n−p)\delta_{n}=O(n^{-p}) with p>1p>1 (Theorem 1), which subsume all practically relevant risk budgets. For the most favorable slowly-decaying schedules, the asymptotic impossibility does not apply, but the tight finite-horizon ceiling (Theorem 5) ensures classifier utility remains subpolynomial — orders of magnitude below a verifier’s linear growth — at any practical deployment horizon.

Why the dual conditions matter for deployed systems. The dual conditions formalize a failure pattern that self-improving systems face by construction. Red-team evaluations — which explicitly classify model outputs or parameter mutations as safe/unsafe — are the closest practical analog to the binary gates our theorems address. Failure to satisfy both conditions simultaneously means either that unsafe modifications accumulate (∑δn\sum\delta_{n} diverges) or that the system stops improving (TPRn→0\mathrm{TPR}_{n}\to 0). Other deployed mechanisms such as RLHF reward models can be viewed as a suggestive analogy, but our formal results apply specifically to binary gates on parameter mutations; for a fuller discussion see §8.1.

1.1 Contributions

The paper establishes two core results and then systematically corroborates them. (Theorems are numbered 1–5 and Propositions 1–4, with separate counters.)

A note on the nature of the contribution. The per-step bound TPRn≤Cα⋅δnβ\mathrm{TPR}_{n}\leq C_{\alpha}\cdot\delta_{n}^{\beta} is a standard f-divergence inequality [27], and the sequential summability consequence follows in a few lines. The proof is short — deliberately so. The contribution of this paper is not the length or technical difficulty of any single proof, but rather: (i) the problem formalization — casting safe self-improvement as dual summability conditions, which has no precedent in the hypothesis testing or AI safety literatures; (ii) the structural consequence — that this elementary coupling creates an impossibility for the safety–utility pairing with no analog in single-test settings; (iii) the tight finite-horizon ceiling (Theorem 5), which provides the exact, universal utility bound for any classifier under any risk schedule; and (iv) the constructive escape via verification, proving the impossibility is specific to classification, not to safe self-improvement itself.

Core results:

  1. 1.

    Classification impossibility (Theorem 1): Any classifier-based gate under distribution overlap satisfies TPRn≤Cα⋅δnβ\mathrm{TPR}_{n}\leq C_{\alpha}\cdot\delta_{n}^{\beta}, forcing bounded utility whenever risk follows a power-law schedule δn=O⁡(n−p)\delta_{n}=O(n^{-p}) with p>1p>1. For slowly-decaying summable sequences (e.g., δn=1/(n​ln2​n)\delta_{n}=1/(n\ln^{2}n)), the per-step bound still holds but the Hölder summability argument does not force ∑TPRn<∞\sum\mathrm{TPR}_{n}<\infty; in such edge cases, the NP-optimal classifier can in principle satisfy both dual conditions simultaneously. However, the finite-horizon ceiling (Theorem 5) remains fully operative in all cases, ensuring classifier utility grows at most subpolynomially — far below a verifier’s linear growth at any practical horizon.

  2. 2.

    Verification escape (Theorem 2): Sound verification gates achieve δ=0\delta=0 with TPR>0\mathrm{TPR}>0, escaping the impossibility. The Lipschitz ball verifier is the simplest example; the structural separation (Proposition 4) proves the gap is architectural, not a matter of degree. See Figure 1 for an overview of the two gate architectures; Figure 6 visualizes the structural separation in the (δ,TPR)(\delta,\mathrm{TPR}) plane.

  3. 3.

    Tight finite-horizon ceiling (Theorem 5): Perhaps the most practically consequential result. For any summable risk schedule — including non-power-law sequences where the Hölder summability argument does not apply — the exact maximum achievable utility is U∗​(N,B)=N⋅TPRNP​(B/N)U^{*}(N,B)=N\cdot\mathrm{TPR}_{\mathrm{NP}}(B/N), growing as exp⁡(O⁡(log⁡N))\exp(O(\sqrt{\log N})). This is subpolynomial, 13×13\times tighter than the MI bound, and ensures that no classifier under any risk schedule can match a verifier’s linear utility growth. Unlike Theorem 1, this result is universal over all summable risk schedules and immediately operational at any finite deployment horizon. See Figure 4.

Tightness and corroboration (confirming the impossibility is robust, not an artifact of one proof technique):

  1. 4.

    Exponent-optimality (Theorem 3): The Hölder exponent β∗\beta^{*} is minimax-optimal — no valid impossibility bound can use a strictly larger exponent. At deployment-relevant δ\delta, the NP classifier operates within one order of magnitude of the ceiling (Appendix D.1). See Figure 3.

  2. 5.

    NP counting impossibility (Theorem 4): An independent proof via the Neyman–Pearson lemma and Tonelli’s theorem, avoiding Hölder’s inequality entirely. The counting bound is 13% tighter than the Hölder bound at Δs=1.0,p=2.0\Delta_{s}=1.0,p=2.0.

Supporting results (extending the theory to information-theoretic, sample complexity, and LLM-scale settings):

  1. 6.

    Information-theoretic bound (Proposition 1): ∑n=1NTPRn≤∑n=1Nδn+2​N​I0\sum_{n=1}^{N}\mathrm{TPR}_{n}\leq\sum_{n=1}^{N}\delta_{n}+\sqrt{2NI_{0}}. Complements the Hölder bound via mutual information.

  2. 7.

    Sample complexity barrier (Proposition 2): Requires Ω⁡(n2​p)\Omega(n^{2p}) labeled examples by step nn; under constant label generation, sample starvation occurs at finite nfailn_{\text{fail}}.

  3. 8.

    Formal transformer Lipschitz bounds (Proposition 3): Closed-form Lipschitz constants for pre-LayerNorm transformers under LoRA, enabling LLM-scale verification.

  4. 9.

    Structural separation (Proposition 4): Under absolute continuity, δ=0⟹TPR=0\delta=0\implies\mathrm{TPR}=0 for classifiers, but verifiers achieve δ=0\delta=0 with TPR>0\mathrm{TPR}>0.

  5. 10.

    LLM-scale mechanism validation: Ball verifier on GPT-2 (124M parameters) with LoRA rank-4 (dLoRA=147,456d_{\text{LoRA}}=147{,}456), achieving conditional δ=0\delta=0 (conditional on estimated Lipschitz constants) with TPR=0.352\mathrm{TPR}=0.352 (§7.1); unconditional δ=0\delta=0 at d≤17,408d\leq 17{,}408 via analytical bounds.

Theorems 3–5 and Propositions 1–4 are corroborative, each confirming the impossibility from a different angle to establish robustness.

1.2 Related Work

Our mathematical tools — Hölder’s inequality, Rényi divergence, Lipschitz continuity, Neyman–Pearson testing — are well-established. The per-step bound TPR≤Cα⋅δβ\mathrm{TPR}\leq C_{\alpha}\cdot\delta^{\beta} is a standard f-divergence inequality [27], and NP optimality [16] establishes single-test ROC tradeoffs. Our contribution is the problem formalization (the dual conditions as a formal specification of safe self-improvement) and the structural result that sequential composition under dual summability conditions creates an impossibility with no analog in single-test settings. The per-step bound and the summability requirements are individually standard; the coupling — that bounded ∑δn\sum\delta_{n} forces bounded ∑TPRn\sum\mathrm{TPR}_{n} for power-law risk schedules — is not, and is confirmed by two independent impossibility proofs (Theorems 1, 4) corroborated by three complementary bounds (Theorem 5, Propositions 1–2) approaching the same conclusion from different angles (§3, §6, Appendix C). We build on alignment theory [6, 2, 7], hypothesis testing [13], impossibility results [30, 21], information-theoretic bounds [20, 19], PAC-Bayes and VC theory [15, 28], adversarial robustness tradeoffs [26, 11], and transformer Lipschitz analysis [29, 12, 8]. Our dual conditions formalize the alignment tax — the cost of making models safe versus capable [3, 17] — as a precise mathematical tradeoff: the Hölder coupling TPRn≤Cα⋅δnβ\mathrm{TPR}_{n}\leq C_{\alpha}\cdot\delta_{n}^{\beta} quantifies the exact rate at which safety constraints reduce utility under classification-based gates. Structurally, our result is closer to mechanism-design impossibilities — Gibbard [10] and Satterthwaite [22] show that no voting rule can simultaneously satisfy multiple natural axioms, just as no classifier can simultaneously satisfy our dual conditions — than to no-free-lunch theorems [30], which concern the absence of a universally optimal learner rather than a hard tradeoff in a fixed domain. Multi-objective optimization impossibilities [18] also exhibit this flavour: two desiderata in conflict cannot be jointly optimized in polynomial time, analogously to how our two summability conditions cannot be jointly satisfied by a classifier under distribution overlap.

A detailed comparison with each line of work is in Appendix B.

An analogy clarifies the contribution. Arrow’s impossibility theorem composes elementary social-choice axioms — transitivity, non-dictatorship, independence — each individually obvious, yet their composition yields a deep impossibility no voting system can escape. Similarly, our per-step bound is a standard f-divergence inequality and the dual conditions are individually natural, but the coupling — that summability of {δn}\{\delta_{n}\} forces summability of {TPRn}\{\mathrm{TPR}_{n}\} — creates a structural impossibility with no analog in single-test hypothesis testing (see Appendix B.1 for a full discussion).

Online learning and adaptive gates. A natural question is whether an online learner with sublinear regret (e.g., online convex optimization; Shalev-Shwartz 24) could adaptively satisfy the dual conditions. The answer is no under our framework: Theorem 1’s per-step bound TPRn≤Cα⋅δnβ\mathrm{TPR}_{n}\leq C_{\alpha}\cdot\delta_{n}^{\beta} constrains any binary decision rule at each step, regardless of whether it was chosen adaptively based on previous observations. Online learning can reduce misclassification regret, but cannot escape the Hölder coupling between δn\delta_{n} and TPRn\mathrm{TPR}_{n} that drives the impossibility. The gate’s adaptivity affects which point on the per-step ROC curve it selects, not the curve itself.

2.1 System Model

A self-improving system maintains parameters θ∈ℝd\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and iteratively proposes mutations θ1,θ2,…\theta_{1},\theta_{2},\ldots At each step nn, a safety oracle S:ℝd→{safe,unsafe}S:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\{\text{safe},\text{unsafe}\} determines ground truth. The oracle is assumed expensive (requiring exhaustive simulation or formal proof).

A safety gate gn:ℝd→{accept,reject}g_{n}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\{\text{accept},\text{reject}\} filters mutations before deployment. The gate is computationally cheaper than the oracle.

2.2 Classification Gates

A classification gate maps controller parameters to a low-dimensional feature representation φ:ℝd→ℝk\varphi:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{k} and applies a binary classifier. The relevant distributions are:

Pn+\displaystyle P_{n}^{+} =distribution of ​φ​(θ)|S⁡(θ)=safe\displaystyle=\text{distribution of }\varphi(\theta)\mid S(\theta)=\text{safe} (1)
Pn−\displaystyle P_{n}^{-} =distribution of ​φ​(θ)|S⁡(θ)=unsafe\displaystyle=\text{distribution of }\varphi(\theta)\mid S(\theta)=\text{unsafe} (2)

At step nn, the gate accepts if the classifier predicts “safe” based on φ⁡(θn)\varphi(\theta_{n}).

Stationarity assumption. The core theorems (§3–§6) assume stationary distributions P+,P−P^{+},P^{-} (dropping the nn subscript). The non-stationary extension (Proposition C.2, Appendix C.2) requires supnDα(n)<∞\sup_{n}D_{\alpha}^{(n)}<\infty and, for power-law schedules δn=c/np\delta_{n}=c/n^{p}, the strictly stronger condition p>αp>\alpha (vs. p>1p>1 in the stationary case). This gap narrows as α→1+\alpha\to 1^{+} and vanishes for fast-decaying schedules (p≫αp\gg\alpha), which cover all practically relevant risk budgets. For deployment arguments where stationarity may not hold and pp is moderate, the finite-horizon ceiling (Theorem 5) provides a stationarity-free alternative: it bounds total classifier utility over any NN-step horizon given a risk budget BB.

Scope: continuous parameter spaces. Our results assume θ∈ℝd\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{d} with continuous mutation distributions, so that P+≪P−P^{+}\ll P^{-} (absolute continuity) holds via the transversality argument (§3.1). For discrete or quantized parameter spaces — such as quantized LoRA fine-tuning with integer-valued weights — absolute continuity does not hold in the same form, and the impossibility may not apply directly. We note that even in quantized settings, the effective parameter updates are typically computed in full precision before rounding, and the induced distributions on the quantized grid can still exhibit the overlap structure that drives our results; a formal treatment of the discrete case is left to future work.

2.3 Verification Gates

A verification gate attempts to construct a mathematical proof that θ\theta is safe. If the proof succeeds, the gate accepts; otherwise it rejects. A key property:

Definition (Soundness).

A verification gate is sound if every accepted θ\theta is actually safe: g⁡(θ)=accept⟹S⁡(θ)=safeg(\theta)=\text{accept}\implies S(\theta)=\text{safe}.

Soundness implies δn=0\delta_{n}=0 for all nn — by construction, not by learning.

2.4 The Dual Conditions

Definition.

A safety gate achieves safe self-improvement if:

  1. 1.

    ∑n=1∞δn<∞\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\delta_{n}<\infty  (bounded cumulative risk)

  2. 2.

    ∑n=1∞TPRn=∞\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\mathrm{TPR}_{n}=\infty  (unbounded cumulative utility)

Condition 1 ensures the system is almost surely safe over infinitely many steps (∏(1−δn)>0\prod(1-\delta_{n})>0 by convergence of the infinite product). Condition 2 prevents vacuous safety (a gate rejecting everything trivially satisfies Condition 1 but accomplishes nothing).

On the choice of ∑TPRn=∞\sum\mathrm{TPR}_{n}=\infty. This is the weakest possible non-vacuity condition: it requires only that the system eventually accepts infinitely many improvements, with no constraint on the rate or timing. Any finite threshold (N0N_{0} accepted modifications “suffice”) is arbitrary and deployment-dependent — a self-improving system has no natural stopping point, and any fixed N0N_{0} can be exceeded by extending the deployment horizon. The condition is also necessary in the following sense: if ∑TPRn<∞\sum\mathrm{TPR}_{n}<\infty, the expected number of accepted improvements is finite, meaning the system almost surely stops self-improving after finitely many steps — it becomes a fixed system with a safety gate that rejects everything beyond some horizon.

Critically, readers who reject the asymptotic framing lose nothing from the theory. Theorem 5 provides the exact finite-horizon utility ceiling U∗​(N,B)=N⋅TPRNP​(B/N)U^{*}(N,B)=N\cdot\mathrm{TPR}_{\mathrm{NP}}(B/N) for any finite NN and risk budget BB, without requiring N→∞N\to\infty. At N=106N=10^{6} steps with B=1.0B=1.0, a classifier extracts at most U∗≈87U^{*}\approx 87 utility versus a verifier’s ≈500,000\approx 500{,}000 — a 5,700×5{,}700\times gap. The dual conditions framework is immediately operational at any finite horizon; the asymptotic condition simply states the limiting case.

3 The Classification Impossibility

3.1 Hölder–Rényi Bound (Theorem 1)

Theorem 1 (Safety–Utility Impossibility).

Let P+,P−P^{+},P^{-} be distributions on ℝk\mathbb{R}^{k} with P+≪P−P^{+}\ll P^{-} (absolute continuity). Suppose Dα0(P+∥P−)<∞D_{\alpha_{0}}(P^{+}\|P^{-})<\infty for some α0>p/(p−1)\alpha_{0}>p/(p-1). Then for any sequence of binary classifiers with false acceptance rates δn≤c/np\delta_{n}\leq c/n^{p} for some c>0,p>1c>0,p>1:

∑n=1∞δn<∞⟹∑n=1∞TPRn<∞\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\delta_{n}<\infty\implies\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\mathrm{TPR}_{n}<\infty

That is, bounded cumulative risk under any power-law schedule forces bounded cumulative utility.

Proof.

Step 1. Let An={x:gn​(x)=accept}A_{n}=\{x:g_{n}(x)=\text{accept}\}. Then:

TPRn=∫And​P+=∫And​P+d​P−​d​P−\mathrm{TPR}_{n}=\int_{A_{n}}dP^{+}=\int_{A_{n}}\frac{dP^{+}}{dP^{-}}dP^{-}

Apply Hölder’s inequality with exponents α>1\alpha>1 and α′=α/(α−1)\alpha^{\prime}=\alpha/(\alpha-1):

TPRn≤(∫An(d​P+d​P−)α​d​P−)1/α⋅(∫And​P−)(α−1)/α\mathrm{TPR}_{n}\leq\left(\int_{A_{n}}\left(\frac{dP^{+}}{dP^{-}}\right)^{\alpha}dP^{-}\right)^{1/\alpha}\cdot\left(\int_{A_{n}}dP^{-}\right)^{(\alpha-1)/\alpha}

Step 2. Bound the first factor by extending the integration domain:

(∫An(d​P+d​P−)αdP−)1/α≤(∫ℝk(d​P+d​P−)αdP−)1/α=exp(α−1αDα(P+∥P−))\left(\int_{A_{n}}\left(\frac{dP^{+}}{dP^{-}}\right)^{\alpha}dP^{-}\right)^{1/\alpha}\leq\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{k}}\left(\frac{dP^{+}}{dP^{-}}\right)^{\alpha}dP^{-}\right)^{1/\alpha}=\exp\left(\frac{\alpha-1}{\alpha}D_{\alpha}(P^{+}\|P^{-})\right)

using the definition Dα(P+∥P−)=1α−1log∫(dP+/dP−)αdP−D_{\alpha}(P^{+}\|P^{-})=\frac{1}{\alpha-1}\log\int(dP^{+}/dP^{-})^{\alpha}\,dP^{-}.

Step 3. Setting β=(α−1)/α∈(0,1)\beta=(\alpha-1)/\alpha\in(0,1) and Cα=exp⁡(β⋅Dα)C_{\alpha}=\exp(\beta\cdot D_{\alpha}):

TPRn≤Cα⋅δnβ\boxed{\mathrm{TPR}_{n}\leq C_{\alpha}\cdot\delta_{n}^{\beta}}

Step 4. If δn=c/np\delta_{n}=c/n^{p} with p>1p>1 (summable), then ∑TPRn≤Cα​cβ​∑n−p​β\sum\mathrm{TPR}_{n}\leq C_{\alpha}c^{\beta}\sum n^{-p\beta}, which converges iff p​β>1p\beta>1. Choose α∈(p/(p−1),α0)\alpha\in(p/(p-1),\,\alpha_{0}) (valid since α0>p/(p−1)\alpha_{0}>p/(p-1) by hypothesis), ensuring p​β>1p\beta>1 and Dα<∞D_{\alpha}<\infty. ∎

Scope and limitations of Theorem 1. The impossibility is established for power-law risk schedules δn=O⁡(n−p)\delta_{n}=O(n^{-p}) with p>1p>1, which subsume all practically relevant risk budgets (geometric, polynomial, or faster decay). For slowly-decaying summable sequences (e.g., δn=1/(n​ln2​n)\delta_{n}=1/(n\ln^{2}n)), the per-step bound TPRn≤Cα⋅δnβ\mathrm{TPR}_{n}\leq C_{\alpha}\cdot\delta_{n}^{\beta} still holds at each step, but ∑Cα​δnβ\sum C_{\alpha}\delta_{n}^{\beta} can diverge because β<1\beta<1 — the Hölder exponent cannot compensate for the slow decay. In such edge cases, the NP-optimal classifier can in principle satisfy both dual conditions simultaneously, and the asymptotic impossibility does not apply. This is an inherent limitation of the Hölder-based proof technique, not an artifact of our analysis.

However, the practical significance of this gap is limited: the finite-horizon ceiling (Theorem 5) remains fully operative for all summable schedules, including these edge cases. Even under the most favorable slowly-decaying schedule, total classifier utility grows at most as exp⁡(O⁡(log⁡N))\exp(O(\sqrt{\log N})) — subpolynomial — while a verifier’s utility grows linearly as Θ⁡(N)\Theta(N) (see §6 for exact bounds). The impossibility is therefore sharp for power-law schedules; the finite-horizon gap is universal.

Two independent impossibility proofs (Theorems 1 and 4) and the exact finite-horizon ceiling (Theorem 5), supported by the information-theoretic rate bound (Proposition 1) and sample complexity barrier (Proposition 2), confirm that the classification ceiling is robust and fundamental, not an artifact of any single proof technique.

Remark (On the per-step bound).

The per-step bound TPRn≤Cα⋅δnβ\mathrm{TPR}_{n}\leq C_{\alpha}\cdot\delta_{n}^{\beta} is a standard f-divergence inequality [27]. The contribution is sequential composition: under summability of {δn}\{\delta_{n}\}, this elementary bound forces ∑TPRn<∞\sum\mathrm{TPR}_{n}<\infty. Two independent proofs (Theorems 1 and 4) and three complementary bounds (Theorem 5, Propositions 1–2) confirm the coupling is robust and technique-independent.

Remark (Necessity of Distribution Overlap).

The assumption P+≪P−P^{+}\ll P^{-} is structurally unavoidable: (i) if safe and unsafe modifications were perfectly separable, the indicator 𝟏supp​(P+)\mathbf{1}_{\text{supp}(P^{+})} would be a zero-error oracle and no gate would be needed; (ii) under full-support mutations and smooth safety boundaries, transversality ensures every feature-space neighborhood contains both safe and unsafe pre-images (see Appendix C for the full geometric argument); (iii) when the safety boundary is piecewise smooth and μ\mu is Gaussian, Dα(P+∥P−)<∞D_{\alpha}(P^{+}\|P^{-})<\infty in a neighborhood of 1. Empirical confirmation: across three systems in [23], measured Δs∈[0.059,0.091]\Delta_{s}\in[0.059,0.091] — well below the separability threshold.

3.2 Exponent-Optimality (Theorem 3)

Theorem 3 (Exponent-Optimality of Hölder Bound).

For Gaussian distributions P+=𝒩⁡(μ,Ik)P^{+}=\mathcal{N}(\mu,I_{k}) and P−=𝒩⁡(0,Ik)P^{-}=\mathcal{N}(0,I_{k}) with separation Δs=‖μ‖\Delta_{s}=\|\mu\|, the Neyman–Pearson optimal classifier achieves TPRNP​(δ)=Φ⁡(Φ−1​(δ)+Δs)\mathrm{TPR}_{\mathrm{NP}}(\delta)=\Phi(\Phi^{-1}(\delta)+\Delta_{s}), and the Hölder exponent β∗=(α∗−1)/α∗\beta^{*}=(\alpha^{*}-1)/\alpha^{*} (with α∗=1+2/Δs2\alpha^{*}=1+2/\Delta_{s}^{2}) is minimax-optimal:

  1. 1.

    No bound TPR≤C′⋅δγ\mathrm{TPR}\leq C^{\prime}\cdot\delta^{\gamma} with γ>β∗\gamma>\beta^{*} is valid uniformly over 𝒫(D,α)={(P+,P−):Dα(P+∥P−)≤D}\mathcal{P}(D,\alpha)=\{(P^{+},P^{-}):D_{\alpha}(P^{+}\|P^{-})\leq D\}.

  2. 2.

    The ratio TPRNP​(δ)/(Cα∗⋅δβ∗)→0\mathrm{TPR}_{\mathrm{NP}}(\delta)/(C_{\alpha^{*}}\cdot\delta^{\beta^{*}})\to 0 as δ→0\delta\to 0 (the NP classifier decays faster than the bound; Appendix A.3), but at deployment-relevant δ∈[10−6,10−1]\delta\in[10^{-6},10^{-1}], the ratio ranges from 0.1 to 0.9 (Appendix D.1).

Proof sketch.

The NP likelihood-ratio test μT​x≷tδ\mu^{T}x\gtrless t_{\delta} yields TPRNP​(δ)=Φ⁡(Φ−1​(δ)+Δs)\mathrm{TPR}_{\mathrm{NP}}(\delta)=\Phi(\Phi^{-1}(\delta)+\Delta_{s}). Asymptotic analysis via Mills’ ratio (Appendix A.3) shows the NP classifier’s log-exponent matches β∗\beta^{*} as an upper envelope: no valid impossibility bound can use a larger exponent. At finite δ\delta values relevant to deployment, TPRNP/Hölder\mathrm{TPR}_{\mathrm{NP}}/\text{H\"{o}lder} ranges from ≈0.1\approx 0.1 (at Δs=2.0\Delta_{s}=2.0) to ≈0.9\approx 0.9 (at Δs=0.1\Delta_{s}=0.1); see Appendix D.1. ∎

Corollary 1 (Minimax Optimality).

The exponent β∗\beta^{*} is minimax-optimal over

𝒫(D,α)={(P+,P−):Dα(P+∥P−)≤D};\mathcal{P}(D,\alpha)=\{(P^{+},P^{-}):D_{\alpha}(P^{+}\|P^{-})\leq D\}\,;

any valid impossibility bound satisfies f⁡(δ)=Ω⁡(δβ∗)f(\delta)=\Omega(\delta^{\beta^{*}}).

The bound is also tight for non-Gaussian distributions: across 8 families (Laplace, Student-tt, Gaussian mixture), the NP classifier achieves 28–70% of the Hölder ceiling (Appendix D.7).

3.3 NP Counting Impossibility (Theorem 4)

We provide a fundamentally different proof of the classification impossibility that avoids Hölder’s inequality and Rényi divergence entirely, using only the Neyman–Pearson lemma and Tonelli’s theorem.

Theorem 4 (NP Counting Impossibility).

Let P+≪P−P^{+}\ll P^{-} with Dα(P+∥P−)<∞D_{\alpha}(P^{+}\|P^{-})<\infty for some α>1\alpha>1. For any summable risk schedule δn=c/np\delta_{n}=c/n^{p} with p>1p>1 and any sequence of classifiers:

∑n=1∞TPRn≤c1/p⋅𝔼P+[P−(L>L(X))−1/p]<∞\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\mathrm{TPR}_{n}\leq c^{1/p}\cdot\mathbb{E}_{P^{+}}\!\left[P^{-}(L>L(X))^{-1/p}\right]<\infty

where L⁡(x)=d​P+/d​P−​(x)L(x)=dP^{+}/dP^{-}(x) is the likelihood ratio.

Proof sketch.

(1) By NP optimality, TPRn≤TPRNP​(δn)\mathrm{TPR}_{n}\leq\mathrm{TPR}_{\mathrm{NP}}(\delta_{n}). (2) Define the counting function N⁡(ℓ)=|{n:cδn<ℓ}|N(\ell)=|\{n:c_{\delta_{n}}<\ell\}|; Tonelli’s theorem gives ∑nTPRNP​(δn)=𝔼P+​[N⁡(L⁡(X))]\sum_{n}\mathrm{TPR}_{\mathrm{NP}}(\delta_{n})=\mathbb{E}_{P^{+}}[N(L(X))]. (3) Bound N⁡(ℓ)≤(c/P−​(L>ℓ))1/pN(\ell)\leq(c/P^{-}(L>\ell))^{1/p}. (4) Finiteness via p-value density integrability. Full proof in Appendix A.8. ∎

The counting bound is strictly tighter than the Hölder bound: 1.76 vs 2.03 at Δs=1.0,p=2.0\Delta_{s}=1.0,p=2.0 (13% improvement). See Appendix D.7 for complete validation including non-Gaussian distributions.

Two additional supporting results are in the appendix: the information-theoretic finite-horizon bound (Proposition 1, Appendix C.3), which constrains the rate of utility accumulation via mutual information (∑TPRn≤∑δn+2​N​I0\sum\mathrm{TPR}_{n}\leq\sum\delta_{n}+\sqrt{2NI_{0}}); and the sample complexity barrier (Proposition 2, Appendix C.4), which shows that learning a gate satisfying the dual conditions requires exponentially growing training sets, independent of Theorem 1. The Gaussian specialization (Appendix C.1) and non-stationary extension with self-correcting structure (Appendix C.2) provide additional theoretical depth.

4 The Verification Escape

4.1 Statement (Theorem 2)

Theorem 2 (Verification Escape).

There exists a verification-based gate achieving:

  • •

    δn=0\delta_{n}=0 for all nn (zero false acceptance)

  • •

    ∑TPRn=∞\sum\mathrm{TPR}_{n}=\infty (unbounded utility)

4.2 Construction: Lipschitz Ball Verifier

Let θ0\theta_{0} be a controller verified safe on a defined operating domain 𝒟={(si,ti)}i=1M\mathcal{D}=\{(s_{i},t_{i})\}_{i=1}^{M} of MM start–target scenarios. Let m>0m>0 be the safety margin: the minimum distance to any obstacle across all scenarios:

m=mini∈[M]⁡mint∈[0,T]⁡d⁡(trajθ0​(t,si,ti),obstacles)m=\min_{i\in[M]}\min_{t\in[0,T]}d(\text{traj}_{\theta_{0}}(t;s_{i},t_{i}),\text{obstacles})

Let LL be a (conservative) Lipschitz constant for the closed-loop trajectory map with respect to controller parameters:

sup(s,t)∈𝒟‖trajθ​(s,t)−trajθ0​(s,t)‖∞≤L⋅‖θ−θ0‖\sup_{(s,t)\in\mathcal{D}}\|\text{traj}_{\theta}(s,t)-\text{traj}_{\theta_{0}}(s,t)\|_{\infty}\leq L\cdot\|\theta-\theta_{0}\|

Ball verifier: Accept θ\theta iff ‖θ−θ0‖<r\|\theta-\theta_{0}\|<r, where r=m/Lr=m/L.

Soundness.

If ‖θ−θ0‖<r\|\theta-\theta_{0}\|<r, then the trajectory deviation is at most L⋅r=mL\cdot r=m. Since θ0\theta_{0} has margin mm, the trajectory of θ\theta stays at distance >0>0 from all obstacles on all scenarios in 𝒟\mathcal{D}. No unsafe controller is accepted. ∎

Remark.

The construction uses standard tools (Lipschitz continuity, the triangle inequality; cf. Berkenkamp et al. 5). The contribution is the quantified dichotomy within the dual conditions framework: the same safety task is provably impossible for any classifier (Theorem 1) yet achievable by a simple O⁡(d)O(d) verifier. Classifiers face a ceiling of exp⁡(O⁡(log⁡N))\exp(O(\sqrt{\log N})) utility (Theorem 5) while verifiers achieve Θ⁡(N)\Theta(N); the structural separation (Proposition 4) establishes that this gap is architectural, not a matter of degree.

Coverage: For mutations Δ​θ∼𝒩⁡(0,σ2​Id)\Delta\theta\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}I_{d}):

TPR=P⁡(‖Δ​θ‖<r)=P⁡(χd2<r2/σ2)\mathrm{TPR}=P(\|\Delta\theta\|<r)=P(\chi^{2}_{d}<r^{2}/\sigma^{2})

This is bounded away from zero when r≥σ​dr\geq\sigma\sqrt{d}, i.e., when m/(L​σ​d)≥1m/(L\sigma\sqrt{d})\geq 1. For smaller mutation scales σ\sigma, TPR→1\mathrm{TPR}\to 1.

Computational cost: The gate checks ‖θ−θ0‖<r\|\theta-\theta_{0}\|<r, an O⁡(d)O(d) operation. No simulation, no oracle calls.

4.3 Domain-Restricted Safety

The verifier guarantees 𝒟\mathcal{D}-safety: safety on a defined operating domain 𝒟\mathcal{D}, standard in formal methods (DO-178C, ISO 26262). A natural objection is that this is weaker than what classifiers attempt — generalization to unseen scenarios. We argue the comparison is more symmetric than it appears.

Classifiers are equally domain-restricted, but probabilistically. Classical generalization bounds [28, 4] guarantee classifier accuracy only on the training distribution 𝒫\mathcal{P}: for a classifier with VC-dimension hh, the empirical risk converges to true risk at rate O⁡(h​log⁡(n)/n)O(\sqrt{h\log(n)/n}) on samples from 𝒫\mathcal{P}. If the operating domain shifts — new obstacle configurations, new task distributions — the classifier requires retraining on the new distribution to maintain its guarantees. This is the statistical analogue of the verifier’s geometric domain restriction.

The guarantee types differ structurally. The verifier’s domain restriction is deterministic: for all θ∈B⁡(θ0,r)\theta\in B(\theta_{0},r) and all scenarios in 𝒟\mathcal{D}, safety holds with certainty (δ=0\delta=0). The classifier’s domain restriction is probabilistic: for most θ\theta drawn from the training distribution, the classifier’s prediction is correct with probability 1−ϵ1-\epsilon. The verifier provides a certificate; the classifier provides a statistical estimate. Both require re-validation if the domain changes, but the verifier’s guarantee within its domain is exact while the classifier’s is approximate.

Both gates face the same test. In the dual conditions framework, both gates are evaluated on mutations from the same distribution P+,P−P^{+},P^{-}; neither has access to out-of-distribution mutations. The Theorem 1 impossibility applies to any binary gate operating on these distributions, regardless of how the gate was trained or whether it generalizes beyond them. The comparison in Theorem 5 — classifier utility exp⁡(O⁡(log⁡N))\exp(O(\sqrt{\log N})) vs. verifier utility Θ⁡(N)\Theta(N) — holds within the shared operating domain.

Formal transformer Lipschitz bounds under LoRA perturbation (Proposition 3) are stated in Appendix C.5 (full derivation in A.7), enabling compositional verification at LLM scale.

5 The Separation Principle (Proposition 4)

Proposition 4 (Structural Classification–Verification Separation).

Under P+≪P−P^{+}\ll P^{-}:

  1. 1.

    For any classifier, δ=0⟹TPR=0\delta=0\implies\mathrm{TPR}=0.

  2. 2.

    There exists a verification gate with δ=0\delta=0 and TPR>0\mathrm{TPR}>0.

  3. 3.

    The separation is strict: as δ→0\delta\to 0, classifiers satisfy TPR→0\mathrm{TPR}\to 0 (Theorem 1), while the verifier maintains constant TPRV>0\mathrm{TPR}_{V}>0 at δV=0\delta_{V}=0 (Theorem 2).

Proof.

(i) If P−​(A)=0P^{-}(A)=0, absolute continuity gives P+​(A)=0P^{+}(A)=0. (ii) The ball B⁡(θ0,r)B(\theta_{0},r) has δ=0\delta=0 (Theorem 2) and positive Gaussian mass. (iii) By Theorem 1, TPRclass​(ϵ)≤Cα​ϵβ→0\mathrm{TPR}_{\text{class}}(\epsilon)\leq C_{\alpha}\epsilon^{\beta}\to 0, while TPRV>0\mathrm{TPR}_{V}>0 is independent of ϵ\epsilon. ∎

Comprehensive experimental validation across 18 classifier configurations ([23] §4.1–4.3), MuJoCo benchmarks ([23] §4.5), and LLM-scale ball chaining ([23] §5.7) is presented in the companion paper [23].

6 Finite-Horizon Analysis

For practical deployment over NN steps with risk budget B=∑δnB=\sum\delta_{n}, we establish the exact utility ceiling.

6.1 Tight Finite-Horizon Ceiling (Theorem 5)

The Hölder–Jensen ceiling Cα⋅N1−β⋅BβC_{\alpha}\cdot N^{1-\beta}\cdot B^{\beta} (Appendix C.6) is not tight: it applies Hölder’s inequality to each step individually and then uses Jensen to optimize allocation. By using the exact NP curve directly, we obtain the tight ceiling.

Theorem 5 (Tight Finite-Horizon Ceiling).

For NN-step deployment with total risk budget B=∑n=1NδnB=\sum_{n=1}^{N}\delta_{n}, the exact maximum achievable utility is:

U∗​(N,B)=N⋅TPRNP​(B/N)U^{*}(N,B)=N\cdot\mathrm{TPR}_{\mathrm{NP}}(B/N)

where TPRNP​(δ)=Φ⁡(Φ−1​(δ)+Δs)\mathrm{TPR}_{\mathrm{NP}}(\delta)=\Phi(\Phi^{-1}(\delta)+\Delta_{s}) is the Neyman–Pearson optimal TPR. The optimal allocation is uniform δn=B/N\delta_{n}=B/N (by concavity of the NP curve and Jensen’s inequality).

For Gaussian distributions with separation Δs\Delta_{s}, the exact growth rate is:

U∗​(N,B)=Θ⁡(exp⁡(Δs​2​ln⁡(N/B))ln⁡(N/B))U^{*}(N,B)=\Theta\!\left(\frac{\exp\!\big(\Delta_{s}\sqrt{2\ln(N/B)}\big)}{\sqrt{\ln(N/B)}}\right)

which is subpolynomial: U∗​(N,B)=o⁡(Nϵ)U^{*}(N,B)=o(N^{\epsilon}) for every ϵ>0\epsilon>0.

Proof.

Step 1 (NP ceiling per step). By the Neyman–Pearson lemma, any classifier at level δn\delta_{n} satisfies TPRn≤TPRNP​(δn)\mathrm{TPR}_{n}\leq\mathrm{TPR}_{\mathrm{NP}}(\delta_{n}). For Gaussians, TPRNP​(δ)=Φ⁡(Φ−1​(δ)+Δs)\mathrm{TPR}_{\mathrm{NP}}(\delta)=\Phi(\Phi^{-1}(\delta)+\Delta_{s}).

Step 2 (Optimal allocation). The ROC curve δ↦TPRNP​(δ)\delta\mapsto\mathrm{TPR}_{\mathrm{NP}}(\delta) is concave (a standard property of NP classifiers under continuous likelihood ratios). By Jensen’s inequality, for any non-negative δ1,…,δN\delta_{1},\ldots,\delta_{N} with ∑δn=B\sum\delta_{n}=B:

∑n=1NTPRNP​(δn)≤N⋅TPRNP​(1N​∑n=1Nδn)=N⋅TPRNP​(B/N)\sum_{n=1}^{N}\mathrm{TPR}_{\mathrm{NP}}(\delta_{n})\leq N\cdot\mathrm{TPR}_{\mathrm{NP}}\!\left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\delta_{n}\right)=N\cdot\mathrm{TPR}_{\mathrm{NP}}(B/N)

This is achieved with equality iff δn=B/N\delta_{n}=B/N for all nn (uniform allocation).

Step 3 (Asymptotic growth). Setting δ=B/N\delta=B/N, as N→∞N\to\infty with BB fixed, δ=B/N→0\delta=B/N\to 0, and by Mills’ ratio:

TPRNP​(B/N)=Φ⁡(Φ−1​(B/N)+Δs)∼e−z2/2z​2​π\mathrm{TPR}_{\mathrm{NP}}(B/N)=\Phi(\Phi^{-1}(B/N)+\Delta_{s})\sim\frac{e^{-z^{2}/2}}{z\sqrt{2\pi}}

where z=2​ln⁡(N/B)−Δsz=\sqrt{2\ln(N/B)}-\Delta_{s}. Thus U∗​(N,B)=N⋅TPRNP​(B/N)U^{*}(N,B)=N\cdot\mathrm{TPR}_{\mathrm{NP}}(B/N) grows as

exp⁡(Δs​2​ln⁡(N/B))ln⁡(N/B)\frac{\exp\!\big(\Delta_{s}\sqrt{2\ln(N/B)}\big)}{\sqrt{\ln(N/B)}}

which is ω⁡(logk⁡N)\omega(\log^{k}N) for all kk but o⁡(Nϵ)o(N^{\epsilon}) for all ϵ>0\epsilon>0. ∎

Comparison of bounds (Gaussian, Δs=1.0\Delta_{s}=1.0, B=1.0B=1.0):

8 Discussion

8.1 Implications for Safe AI Deployment

Theorem 1 implies that any AI safety approach based on classifying modifications — learned discriminators, anomaly detectors, neural safety critics — faces a fundamental ceiling that is a mathematical consequence of distribution overlap, not a limitation of architecture or training. To the extent that RLHF reward models act as binary accept/reject gates after thresholding, they inherit this ceiling (see §1 for the analogy and its limits; the formal results strictly apply to binary gates on parameter mutations, not continuous reward scores). Over sufficient iterations, either the false acceptance rate accumulates (safety degrades) or the gate becomes overly conservative (utility collapses).

We address five common concerns.

“∑TPRn=∞\sum\mathrm{TPR}_{n}=\infty is too weak.” Even this weak condition cannot be met with bounded risk; strengthening it (requiring TPRn≥c>0\mathrm{TPR}_{n}\geq c>0) forces δn≥(c/Cα)1/β\delta_{n}\geq(c/C_{\alpha})^{1/\beta} for all nn, making ∑δn\sum\delta_{n} diverge immediately.

“Finite-time systems don’t need ∑TPRn=∞\sum\mathrm{TPR}_{n}=\infty.” The finite-horizon tradeoff still applies: with risk budget BB, total utility grows subpolynomially (Theorem 5), yielding an exact budget-allocation formula for finite deployments.

“Classifiers still extract nonzero utility.” Correct — but the ceiling is subpolynomial (exp⁡(O⁡(log⁡N))\exp(O(\sqrt{\log N}))) versus the verifier’s linear growth (Θ⁡(N)\Theta(N)). At N=10,000N=10{,}000 with B=1.0B=1.0, a classifier extracts U∗≈32.7U^{*}\approx 32.7 versus a ball verifier’s Uball=5,000U_{\text{ball}}=5{,}000 — a 153×\times advantage (Appendix D.10). “Impossibility” refers to satisfying the dual conditions simultaneously, not to extracting any utility at all.

“What about an ensemble of diverse classifiers?” An ensemble accepting iff all members agree is itself a classifier with acceptance region A=⋂iAiA=\bigcap_{i}A_{i}. Theorem 1 applies: TPRn≤Cα⋅δnβ\mathrm{TPR}_{n}\leq C_{\alpha}\cdot\delta_{n}^{\beta} constrains any binary decision rule. The impossibility is driven by β<1\beta<1, not classifier complexity.

“Isn’t the verifier’s conditional δ=0\delta=0 just as uncertain as a classifier’s δ≈0\delta\approx 0?” No — the failure modes are categorically different. A classifier’s δ>0\delta>0 is a mathematical necessity under distribution overlap (Theorem 1); no amount of better training, data, or architecture can achieve δ=0\delta=0 with TPR>0\mathrm{TPR}>0 (Proposition 4). The verifier’s conditionality rests on the Lipschitz constant being correct — a falsifiable engineering claim that strengthens monotonically with better estimation. At d≤17,408d\leq 17{,}408, we provide analytical bounds making δ=0\delta=0 unconditional; at LLM scale, Proposition 3 proves the required bound exists and the open problem is computing it tractably. The distinction is between an impossibility theorem and an open engineering problem (see [23] §6.3).

The classification–verification separation mirrors behavioral testing versus formal guarantees. Current AI safety practices — red-teaming, evaluations, benchmarks — are primarily classification-based; as self-modification becomes prevalent, verification-based safety will be mathematically required.

Remark (Overlap under mutation-specific distributions).

Even if mutations come from a specific distribution μ\mu, the induced conditional distributions P+=μ|safeP^{+}=\mu|_{\text{safe}} and P−=μ|unsafeP^{-}=\mu|_{\text{unsafe}} satisfy P+≪P−P^{+}\ll P^{-} by the transversality argument (§3.1), and the Hölder ceiling applies parametrically. The companion paper [23] measures Δs∈[0.059,0.091]\Delta_{s}\in[0.059,0.091] across three physical systems (§4.5), confirming low separation.

Connections to computational complexity (is satisfying the dual conditions NP-hard?) and open problems (adaptive verification, multi-agent extensions) are discussed in Appendix E.

8.2 When Our Results Do Not Apply

The impossibility (Theorem 1) and the finite-horizon ceiling (Theorem 5) require specific structural conditions. Practitioners should evaluate whether their setting satisfies these conditions before applying our conclusions:

  1. 1.

    Perfectly separable distributions. If safe and unsafe modifications are perfectly separable in feature space (Dα(P+∥P−)=∞D_{\alpha}(P^{+}\|P^{-})=\infty or equivalently P+⟂P−P^{+}\perp P^{-}), the Hölder bound becomes vacuous and a perfect classifier can achieve δ=0\delta=0 with TPR=1\mathrm{TPR}=1. This occurs when the safety boundary does not pass through the support of the mutation distribution. Our results apply only when P+P^{+} and P−P^{-} have overlapping support (§3.1).

  2. 2.

    Discrete or quantized parameter spaces. Our framework assumes continuous parameter perturbations from distributions with density. If the parameter space is finite or modifications come from a discrete set, the safe/unsafe partition may be exactly learnable and the distribution overlap condition may not hold.

  3. 3.

    Large safety margins with small modification sets. If the system operates far from any safety boundary and modifications are bounded to a region where all points are safe, no gate is needed at all. Our results address the non-trivial regime where safety boundaries intersect the modification space.

  4. 4.

    Fixed finite deployments where classifier utility suffices. Theorem 5 shows classifier utility grows as exp⁡(O⁡(log⁡N))\exp(O(\sqrt{\log N})), which is non-zero. For short deployment horizons — say N≤100N\leq 100 with a generous risk budget BB — a classifier may provide adequate utility even under the Hölder ceiling. The impossibility becomes practically binding only when NN is large enough that the subpolynomial ceiling falls far below the linear growth a verifier achieves.

  5. 5.

    Systems with non-overlapping mutation distributions by design. Some safety mechanisms engineer the modification space to avoid overlap — for example, restricting updates to a pre-verified subspace. If the restriction is enforced before the gate, the resulting conditional distributions may be separable, and a classifier within this restricted space may succeed. Our framework applies to the unrestricted case.

9 Conclusion

For power-law risk schedules δn=O⁡(n−p)\delta_{n}=O(n^{-p}) with p>1p>1 — the practically relevant regime — classifier-based safety gates cannot satisfy the dual conditions under any architecture, training regime, or data availability. This is established through two independent impossibility proofs (Theorems 1 and 4), proved exponent-optimal by the NP matching lower bound (Theorem 3; Mills’ ratio asymptotics in Appendix A.3), and corroborated by two complementary bounds: the information-theoretic rate bound (Proposition 1) and the sample complexity barrier (Proposition 2). For slowly-decaying non-power-law schedules where the asymptotic impossibility does not hold, Theorem 5’s universal finite-horizon ceiling ensures classifier utility grows at most as exp⁡(O⁡(log⁡N))\exp(O(\sqrt{\log N})) — orders of magnitude below a verifier’s linear Θ⁡(N)\Theta(N) growth at any practical horizon. A constructive escape via sound verification gates (Theorem 2) achieves δ=0\delta=0 with TPR>0\mathrm{TPR}>0; the separation is strict (Proposition 4). We validate on GPT-2 with LoRA (d=147,456d=147{,}456): the ball verifier achieves conditional δ=0\delta=0 (unconditional at d≤17,408d\leq 17{,}408) with TPR=0.352\mathrm{TPR}=0.352 (§7.1). Comprehensive experimental validation is in the companion paper [23].

Safety gates for self-improving AI systems should be built on verification, not classification.

Appendix A Proof Details

A.1 Hölder Inequality Verification

The conjugate exponents α\alpha and α′=α/(α−1)\alpha^{\prime}=\alpha/(\alpha-1) satisfy 1/α+1/α′=11/\alpha+1/\alpha^{\prime}=1. The Hölder inequality:

∫f​g≤‖f‖α⋅‖g‖α′\int fg\leq\|f\|_{\alpha}\cdot\|g\|_{\alpha^{\prime}}

is applied with f=d​P+/d​P−f=dP^{+}/dP^{-} and g=𝟏Ang=\mathbf{1}_{A_{n}}, both measured against P−P^{-}. Then:

TPRn=∫And​P+=∫And​P+d​P−​d​P−=∫f​g​d​P−\mathrm{TPR}_{n}=\int_{A_{n}}dP^{+}=\int_{A_{n}}\frac{dP^{+}}{dP^{-}}dP^{-}=\int fg\,dP^{-}

By Hölder:

TPRn≤(∫(d​P+d​P−)α​d​P−)1/α⋅(∫𝟏Anα′​d​P−)1/α′\mathrm{TPR}_{n}\leq\left(\int\left(\frac{dP^{+}}{dP^{-}}\right)^{\alpha}dP^{-}\right)^{1/\alpha}\cdot\left(\int\mathbf{1}_{A_{n}}^{\alpha^{\prime}}dP^{-}\right)^{1/\alpha^{\prime}}

The first factor is e(α−1)Dα(P+∥P−)/α=Cαe^{(\alpha-1)D_{\alpha}(P^{+}\|P^{-})/\alpha}=C_{\alpha} (by definition of Rényi divergence). The second factor is δn1/α′=δn(α−1)/α=δnβ\delta_{n}^{1/\alpha^{\prime}}=\delta_{n}^{(\alpha-1)/\alpha}=\delta_{n}^{\beta}.

A.2 Rényi Divergence Convention

We use Dα(P∥Q)=1α−1log∫(dP/dQ)αdQD_{\alpha}(P\|Q)=\frac{1}{\alpha-1}\log\int(dP/dQ)^{\alpha}\,dQ following van Erven and Harremoes [27]. This differs from some references by a factor of (α−1)(\alpha-1) in the exponent. The constant Cα=exp(α−1αDα(P+∥P−))C_{\alpha}=\exp\!\bigl(\frac{\alpha-1}{\alpha}D_{\alpha}(P^{+}\|P^{-})\bigr) is finite whenever the Rényi divergence is finite, which requires P+≪P−P^{+}\ll P^{-} (absolute continuity) and sufficiently light tails of the likelihood ratio.

A.3 Theorem 3 Exponent-Optimality: Mills’ Ratio Asymptotics

We provide the full asymptotic analysis establishing the exponent-optimality of the Hölder bound.

Setup. For Gaussian P+=𝒩⁡(μ,Ik)P^{+}=\mathcal{N}(\mu,I_{k}), P−=𝒩⁡(0,Ik)P^{-}=\mathcal{N}(0,I_{k}) with Δs=‖μ‖\Delta_{s}=\|\mu\|, the NP optimal test rejects when μT​x<tδ\mu^{T}x<t_{\delta}, giving TPRNP​(δ)=Φ⁡(Φ−1​(δ)+Δs)\mathrm{TPR}_{\mathrm{NP}}(\delta)=\Phi(\Phi^{-1}(\delta)+\Delta_{s}) where Φ\Phi is the standard normal CDF. The Hölder bound with optimal order α∗=1+2/Δs2\alpha^{*}=1+2/\Delta_{s}^{2} and β∗=1−1/α∗=2/(2+Δs2)\beta^{*}=1-1/\alpha^{*}=2/(2+\Delta_{s}^{2}) gives Cα∗=exp⁡(Δs2/2)C_{\alpha^{*}}=\exp(\Delta_{s}^{2}/2).

Log-asymptotic analysis. As δ→0\delta\to 0, set zδ=Φ−1​(1−δ)z_{\delta}=\Phi^{-1}(1-\delta) (so zδ→+∞z_{\delta}\to+\infty). Comparing the log-exponents directly:

log⁡TPRNP​(δ)∼−(zδ−Δs)22,log⁡(Cα∗​δβ∗)∼Δs22−β∗​zδ22\log\mathrm{TPR}_{\mathrm{NP}}(\delta)\sim-\frac{(z_{\delta}-\Delta_{s})^{2}}{2},\qquad\log(C_{\alpha^{*}}\delta^{\beta^{*}})\sim\frac{\Delta_{s}^{2}}{2}-\frac{\beta^{*}z_{\delta}^{2}}{2}

Dividing by logδ∼−zδ2/2\log\delta\sim-z_{\delta}^{2}/2:

log⁡TPRNP​(δ)log⁡δ→(zδ−Δs)2zδ2=1−2​Δszδ+Δs2zδ2→1\frac{\log\mathrm{TPR}_{\mathrm{NP}}(\delta)}{\log\delta}\to\frac{(z_{\delta}-\Delta_{s})^{2}}{z_{\delta}^{2}}=1-\frac{2\Delta_{s}}{z_{\delta}}+\frac{\Delta_{s}^{2}}{z_{\delta}^{2}}\to 1

while log⁡(Cα∗​δβ∗)log⁡δ→β∗<1\frac{\log(C_{\alpha^{*}}\delta^{\beta^{*}})}{\log\delta}\to\beta^{*}<1. Since the NP classifier’s log-exponent (1) exceeds the Hölder bound’s (β∗\beta^{*}), the ratio TPRNP​(δ)/(Cα∗​δβ∗)→0\mathrm{TPR}_{\mathrm{NP}}(\delta)/(C_{\alpha^{*}}\delta^{\beta^{*}})\to 0 as δ→0\delta\to 0 — the NP classifier decays faster than the bound.

Exponent-optimality. The key consequence:

lim infδ→0log⁡TPRNP​(δ)log⁡δ=1>β∗\liminf_{\delta\to 0}\frac{\log\mathrm{TPR}_{\mathrm{NP}}(\delta)}{\log\delta}=1>\beta^{*}

The NP classifier achieves TPR=Ω⁡(δ1−ϵ)\mathrm{TPR}=\Omega(\delta^{1-\epsilon}) for all ϵ>0\epsilon>0, so any valid universal upper bound must have exponent ≤1\leq 1. Meanwhile, the Hölder bound with β∗<1\beta^{*}<1 is valid. Therefore β∗\beta^{*} is the smallest exponent achievable by any impossibility bound — it cannot be replaced by any γ>β∗\gamma>\beta^{*} without violating the NP classifier’s performance. ∎

Practical tightness. At finite δ\delta values relevant to deployment (δ∈[10−6,10−1]\delta\in[10^{-6},10^{-1}]), the ratio TPRNP/(Cα∗​δβ∗)\mathrm{TPR}_{\mathrm{NP}}/(C_{\alpha^{*}}\delta^{\beta^{*}}) ranges from 0.1 to 0.9 depending on Δs\Delta_{s} (Appendix D.1), confirming that the bound is practically tight — the NP classifier operates within one order of magnitude of the Hölder ceiling across the deployment-relevant range.

Suppose θ∈B⁡(θ0,r)\theta\in B(\theta_{0},r) with r=m/Lr=m/L. For any scenario (si,ti)∈𝒟(s_{i},t_{i})\in\mathcal{D}:

suptd⁡(trajθ​(t),trajθ0​(t))≤L⋅‖θ−θ0‖<L⋅r=m\sup_{t}d(\text{traj}_{\theta}(t),\text{traj}_{\theta_{0}}(t))\leq L\cdot\|\theta-\theta_{0}\|<L\cdot r=m

Since θ0\theta_{0} has margin mm (minimum distance to obstacles), the trajectory of θ\theta maintains positive distance to all obstacles:

d⁡(trajθ​(t),obstaclej)≥m−L​‖θ−θ0‖>0∀t,jd(\text{traj}_{\theta}(t),\text{obstacle}_{j})\geq m-L\|\theta-\theta_{0}\|>0\quad\forall t,j

Therefore θ\theta is 𝒟\mathcal{D}-safe. ∎

A.5 Information-Theoretic Bound Full Proof

Setup. At each step nn, the gate gn:ℝk→{accept,reject}g_{n}:\mathbb{R}^{k}\to\{\text{accept},\text{reject}\} induces a binary channel from the safety label Sn∈{safe,unsafe}S_{n}\in\{\text{safe},\text{unsafe}\} to the gate decision. The mutual information of this channel is:

In=I⁡(gn​(θn),Sn)=H⁡(gn)−H⁡(gn|Sn)I_{n}=I(g_{n}(\theta_{n});S_{n})=H(g_{n})-H(g_{n}|S_{n})

Pinsker bound. The total variation between the gate’s conditional distributions satisfies TV⁡(Pg|+,Pg|−)=|TPRn−δn|/2\mathrm{TV}(P_{g|+},P_{g|-})=|\mathrm{TPR}_{n}-\delta_{n}|/2. By Pinsker’s inequality:

|TPRn−δn|2≤In2\frac{|\mathrm{TPR}_{n}-\delta_{n}|}{2}\leq\sqrt{\frac{I_{n}}{2}}

Hence TPRn≤δn+2​In\mathrm{TPR}_{n}\leq\delta_{n}+\sqrt{2I_{n}}.

Summation. Summing over n=1,…,Nn=1,\ldots,N:

∑n=1NTPRn≤∑n=1Nδn+∑n=1N2​In\sum_{n=1}^{N}\mathrm{TPR}_{n}\leq\sum_{n=1}^{N}\delta_{n}+\sum_{n=1}^{N}\sqrt{2I_{n}}

By Cauchy–Schwarz: ∑n=1NIn≤N​∑n=1NIn\sum_{n=1}^{N}\sqrt{I_{n}}\leq\sqrt{N\sum_{n=1}^{N}I_{n}}. Under the bounded mutual information assumption ∑n=1NIn≤I0\sum_{n=1}^{N}I_{n}\leq I_{0}:

∑n=1NTPRn≤∑n=1Nδn+2​N​I0∎\sum_{n=1}^{N}\mathrm{TPR}_{n}\leq\sum_{n=1}^{N}\delta_{n}+\sqrt{2NI_{0}}\qed

Setup. The safety gate at step nn is a binary classifier gn∈𝒢g_{n}\in\mathcal{G} (a hypothesis class with VC dimension dVCd_{\text{VC}}), trained on ntrain​(n)n_{\text{train}}(n) labeled examples.

Step 1: By the fundamental theorem of statistical learning [28, 13], with probability ≥1−η\geq 1-\eta: errtrue≤errtrain+(dVC​ln⁡(2​m/dVC)+ln⁡(2/η))/m\text{err}_{\text{true}}\leq\text{err}_{\text{train}}+\sqrt{(d_{\text{VC}}\ln(2m/d_{\text{VC}})+\ln(2/\eta))/m}.

Step 2: Setting the bound equal to ϵn/2\epsilon_{n}/2 and solving: ntrain​(n)=Ω⁡(dVC/ϵn2)n_{\text{train}}(n)=\Omega(d_{\text{VC}}/\epsilon_{n}^{2}).

Step 3: For ϵn=c/np\epsilon_{n}=c/n^{p}: ntrain​(n)=Ω⁡(dVC⋅n2​p/c2)n_{\text{train}}(n)=\Omega(d_{\text{VC}}\cdot n^{2p}/c^{2}).

Step 4: Available data grows as n0+k​nn_{0}+kn; required data as n2​pn^{2p}. The crossing point: nfail=Θ⁡((c2​k/dVC)1/(2​p−1))n_{\text{fail}}=\Theta((c^{2}k/d_{\text{VC}})^{1/(2p-1)}). ∎

We derive the per-layer Lipschitz constant for a pre-LayerNorm transformer under LoRA perturbation of attention projections. Each layer kk computes:

yk=xk+MHA​(LN1​(xk)),zk=yk+FFN​(LN2​(yk))y_{k}=x_{k}+\text{MHA}(\text{LN}_{1}(x_{k})),\quad z_{k}=y_{k}+\text{FFN}(\text{LN}_{2}(y_{k}))

LkLoRA≤‖γk‖ϵ⋅maxp⁡‖Wv,p0‖dk⋅2​nprojL_{k}^{\text{LoRA}}\leq\frac{\|\gamma_{k}\|}{\sqrt{\epsilon}}\cdot\frac{\max_{p}\|W_{v,p}^{0}\|}{\sqrt{d_{k}}}\cdot\sqrt{2n_{\text{proj}}}

‖Δ​output‖≤∑k=1KLkLoRA⋅‖Δ​θk‖⋅∏j>kLjfull,frozen\|\Delta\text{output}\|\leq\sum_{k=1}^{K}L_{k}^{\text{LoRA}}\cdot\|\Delta\theta_{k}\|\cdot\prod_{j>k}L_{j}^{\text{full,frozen}}

A.8 NP Counting Proof Full Details

Tonelli interchange. The interchange ∑nP+​(L⁡(X)>cδn)=𝔼P+​[∑n𝟏L⁡(X)>cδn]\sum_{n}P^{+}(L(X)>c_{\delta_{n}})=\mathbb{E}_{P^{+}}[\sum_{n}\mathbf{1}_{L(X)>c_{\delta_{n}}}] is justified by Tonelli’s theorem applied to non-negative measurable functions with the counting measure on ℕ\mathbb{N} and P+P^{+} on ℝk\mathbb{R}^{k}.

Counting function. N⁡(ℓ)=|{n∈ℕ:cδn<ℓ}|N(\ell)=|\{n\in\mathbb{N}:c_{\delta_{n}}<\ell\}| counts how many thresholds are exceeded. For δn=c/np\delta_{n}=c/n^{p}, we get N⁡(ℓ)≤(c/P−​(L>ℓ))1/pN(\ell)\leq(c/P^{-}(L>\ell))^{1/p}.

P-value density integrability. Writing U⁡(x)=P−​(L>L⁡(x))U(x)=P^{-}(L>L(x)), the bound becomes 𝔼P+[U(X)−1/p]\mathbb{E}_{P^{+}}[U(X)^{-1/p}]. For p>1p>1, the integrand u−1/pfU(u)u^{-1/p}f_{U}(u) is integrable near u=0u=0 because the Gaussian tail makes fU​(u)f_{U}(u) decay super-polynomially. More generally, the expectation is finite whenever the p-value density satisfies fU​(u)=O⁡(uη)f_{U}(u)=O(u^{\eta}) near u=0u=0 for some η>1/p−1\eta>1/p-1; this holds for all distribution pairs with Dα(P+∥P−)<∞D_{\alpha}(P^{+}\|P^{-})<\infty for sufficiently large α\alpha, which is guaranteed by the hypothesis of Theorem 4. ∎

A.9 Tight Finite-Horizon Ceiling Details

Concavity of NP curve. The derivative TPRNP′​(δ)=ϕ⁡(Φ−1​(δ)+Δs)/ϕ⁡(Φ−1​(δ))\mathrm{TPR}_{\mathrm{NP}}^{\prime}(\delta)=\phi(\Phi^{-1}(\delta)+\Delta_{s})/\phi(\Phi^{-1}(\delta)). The second derivative is negative for all δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1) by log-concavity of ϕ\phi, establishing concavity (see also [13], Chapter 3).

Asymptotic formula. Using Φ−1​(δ)∼−2​ln⁡(1/δ)\Phi^{-1}(\delta)\sim-\sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta)} for δ→0\delta\to 0 and Mills’ ratio:

U∗​(N,B)∼B⋅exp⁡(Δs​2​ln⁡(N/B)−Δs2/2)2​π⋅2​ln⁡(N/B)U^{*}(N,B)\sim\frac{B\cdot\exp(\Delta_{s}\sqrt{2\ln(N/B)}-\Delta_{s}^{2}/2)}{\sqrt{2\pi\cdot 2\ln(N/B)}}

This grows as exp⁡(Δs​2​ln⁡(N/B))\exp(\Delta_{s}\sqrt{2\ln(N/B)}), which is o⁡(Nϵ)o(N^{\epsilon}) for every ϵ>0\epsilon>0 but ω⁡(logk⁡N)\omega(\log^{k}N) for every kk. ∎

Appendix B Relation to Known Results and Extended Related Work

B.1 Relation to Known Results

The mathematical tools in this paper — Hölder’s inequality, Rényi divergence, Lipschitz continuity, Fano’s inequality, VC dimension — are well-established. The per-step bound TPR≤Cα⋅δβ\mathrm{TPR}\leq C_{\alpha}\cdot\delta^{\beta} is an instance of a standard f-divergence inequality [27], and the Neyman–Pearson lemma [16] establishes ROC tradeoffs for individual hypothesis tests.

Our contribution is the problem formalization and the structural results that emerge: (1) the dual conditions as a formalization of safe self-improvement, (2) sequential composition creating an impossibility for the coupling of bounded risk and unbounded utility, (3) the tightness of this coupling, (4) its information-theoretic strengthening, (5) the sample complexity barrier, and (6) the structural separation between classification and verification.

An analogy clarifies the distinction. Arrow’s impossibility theorem uses elementary social-choice axioms, each individually obvious, but their composition yields a deep impossibility no voting system can escape. Similarly, our per-step bound is standard, and the dual conditions are individually natural. But the coupling creates a structural impossibility with no analog in single-test hypothesis testing.

B.2 Extended Related Work

Self-improving AI safety. The alignment literature discusses recursive self-improvement [6, 25] and concrete safety challenges [2] but lacks formal impossibility results for the safety–utility coupling. Christiano et al. [7] propose iterated amplification; Leike et al. [14] formalize reward modeling.

Hypothesis testing and statistical tradeoffs. The Neyman–Pearson lemma [16, 13] establishes optimal ROC tradeoffs for individual tests. The novelty is sequential composition: summability constraints on {δn}\{\delta_{n}\} force summability on {TPRn}\{\mathrm{TPR}_{n}\}.

Impossibility results in learning theory. No-free-lunch theorems [30] show no classifier dominates across all distributions. Rice [21] shows undecidability of semantic properties. Our impossibility is for a specific task under distribution overlap.

Information-theoretic bounds. Fano’s inequality and its refinements [20] provide fundamental limits. The strong data processing inequality [19, 1] bounds information processing gains.

PAC-Bayes and sample complexity. McAllester [15] bound generalization via KL divergence. Vapnik and Chervonenkis [28] established VC dimension. We use VC sample complexity to show independent barriers.

Adversarial robustness. Tsipras et al. [26] prove accuracy–robustness tradeoffs. Gilmer et al. [11] show adversarial examples are inevitable in high dimensions. Our impossibility concerns sequential composition, not per-input robustness.

Transformer Lipschitz bounds. Virmaux and Scaman [29] compute spectral norms. Kim et al. [12] analyze attention Lipschitz properties. Dasoulas et al. [8] study Lipschitz normalization. Fazlyab et al. [9] use SDP for tight bounds. We derive bounds for LoRA perturbations specifically.

Appendix C Supporting Theoretical Results

C.1 Gaussian Specialization

For unit-variance Gaussians with separation Δs=|μ+−μ−|/σ\Delta_{s}=|\mu^{+}-\mu^{-}|/\sigma: Dα(P+∥P−)=αΔs2/2D_{\alpha}(P^{+}\|P^{-})=\alpha\,\Delta_{s}^{2}/2. The optimal (Neyman–Pearson) classifier achieves TPR=Φ⁡(Φ−1​(δ)+Δs)\mathrm{TPR}=\Phi(\Phi^{-1}(\delta)+\Delta_{s}).

C.2 Non-Stationary Extension

Proposition C.2 (Non-Stationary Impossibility).

Let {(Pn+,Pn−)}n≥1\{(P_{n}^{+},P_{n}^{-})\}_{n\geq 1} be a sequence of distribution pairs and α∈(1,∞)\alpha\in(1,\infty) with β=1−1/α\beta=1-1/\alpha. Suppose D¯:=supnDα(Pn+∥Pn−)<∞\bar{D}:=\sup_{n}D_{\alpha}(P_{n}^{+}\|P_{n}^{-})<\infty. Then for any sequence of classifiers {gn}\{g_{n}\} with per-step rates (δn,TPRn)(\delta_{n},\mathrm{TPR}_{n}):

TPRn≤C¯α⋅δnβfor all ​n\mathrm{TPR}_{n}\leq\bar{C}_{\alpha}\cdot\delta_{n}^{\beta}\quad\text{for all }n

where C¯α=exp⁡((α−1)​D¯)\bar{C}_{\alpha}=\exp((\alpha-1)\bar{D}). Consequently, if ∑δn<∞\sum\delta_{n}<\infty then ∑TPRn≤C¯α​∑δnβ<∞\sum\mathrm{TPR}_{n}\leq\bar{C}_{\alpha}\sum\delta_{n}^{\beta}<\infty, and the dual conditions cannot be jointly satisfied.

Proof.

At each step nn, the Hölder bound (Theorem 1 proof, Step 1) gives TPRn≤Cα(n)⋅δnβ\mathrm{TPR}_{n}\leq C_{\alpha}^{(n)}\cdot\delta_{n}^{\beta} where Cα(n)=exp((α−1)Dα(Pn+∥Pn−))C_{\alpha}^{(n)}=\exp((\alpha-1)D_{\alpha}(P_{n}^{+}\|P_{n}^{-})). Since Dα(Pn+∥Pn−)≤D¯D_{\alpha}(P_{n}^{+}\|P_{n}^{-})\leq\bar{D} for all nn, we have Cα(n)≤C¯αC_{\alpha}^{(n)}\leq\bar{C}_{\alpha}. Summing: ∑TPRn≤C¯α​∑δnβ\sum\mathrm{TPR}_{n}\leq\bar{C}_{\alpha}\sum\delta_{n}^{\beta}. For power-law schedules δn≤c/np\delta_{n}\leq c/n^{p}, we have δnβ≤cβ​n−p​β\delta_{n}^{\beta}\leq c^{\beta}n^{-p\beta}, which is summable iff p​β>1p\beta>1 (i.e., p>αp>\alpha). For general summable {δn}\{\delta_{n}\}, convergence of ∑δnβ\sum\delta_{n}^{\beta} follows from Hölder’s inequality on finite horizons: ∑n=1Nδnβ≤N1−β⋅(∑n=1Nδn)β≤N1−β⋅Bβ\sum_{n=1}^{N}\delta_{n}^{\beta}\leq N^{1-\beta}\cdot(\sum_{n=1}^{N}\delta_{n})^{\beta}\leq N^{1-\beta}\cdot B^{\beta} where B=∑δn<∞B=\sum\delta_{n}<\infty. ∎

Remark (Coverage gap).

For power-law schedules δn=c⋅n−p\delta_{n}=c\cdot n^{-p} with p>1p>1, the series ∑δnβ=cβ​∑n−p​β\sum\delta_{n}^{\beta}=c^{\beta}\sum n^{-p\beta} converges iff p​β>1p\beta>1, i.e., p>αp>\alpha. For 1<p≤α1<p\leq\alpha, the stationary impossibility (Theorem 1) applies but Proposition C.2 does not — the non-stationary extension requires the strictly stronger condition p>αp>\alpha (flagged in §2.2). This gap narrows as α→1+\alpha\to 1^{+} and vanishes for all practically relevant fast-decaying schedules (p≥2p\geq 2). For the intermediate regime, Theorem 5’s stationarity-free finite-horizon ceiling provides an alternative bound.

C.3 Information-Theoretic Finite-Horizon Bound

Proposition 1 (Information-Theoretic Finite-Horizon Bound).

Let {gn}\{g_{n}\} be a sequence of safety gates with per-step mutual information InI_{n} and total budget I0=∑InI_{0}=\sum I_{n}. Then for any NN:

∑n=1NTPRn≤∑n=1Nδn+2​N​I0\sum_{n=1}^{N}\mathrm{TPR}_{n}\leq\sum_{n=1}^{N}\delta_{n}+\sqrt{2NI_{0}}

This bound grows as N\sqrt{N}, so it does not prove ∑TPRn<∞\sum\mathrm{TPR}_{n}<\infty — that follows from Theorem 1. Proposition 1 complements Theorem 1 by constraining the rate of utility accumulation via mutual information. Full proof in Appendix A.5.

C.4 Sample Complexity Barrier

Proposition 2 (Sample Complexity Barrier).

Let 𝒢\mathcal{G} be a family of binary classifiers with VC dimension dVCd_{\text{VC}}. For the gate to achieve δn≤c/np\delta_{n}\leq c/n^{p} with p>1p>1, the required training set is ntrain​(n)=Ω⁡(dVC⋅n2​p)n_{\text{train}}(n)=\Omega(d_{\text{VC}}\cdot n^{2p}). If the system generates at most kk new labeled examples per step, sample starvation occurs at nfail=O⁡(k1/(2​p−1))n_{\text{fail}}=O(k^{1/(2p-1)}).

This result is independent of Theorem 1: even if a classifier circumvented the Hölder bound, it would face sample starvation. Full proof in Appendix A.6.

C.5 Formal Transformer Lipschitz Bounds

Proposition 3 (Transformer LoRA Lipschitz Bound).

For a pre-LayerNorm transformer with KK layers under LoRA perturbation with rank rr on nprojn_{\text{proj}} attention projections per layer, the per-layer Lipschitz constant w.r.t. LoRA parameters is:

LkLoRA≤‖γk‖ϵ⋅maxp⁡‖Wv,p0‖dk⋅2⋅nprojL_{k}^{\text{LoRA}}\leq\frac{\|\gamma_{k}\|}{\sqrt{\epsilon}}\cdot\frac{\max_{p}\|W_{v,p}^{0}\|}{\sqrt{d_{k}}}\cdot\sqrt{2\cdot n_{\text{proj}}}

Compositional verification checks ∑kLkLoRA⋅‖Δ​θk‖≤m\sum_{k}L_{k}^{\text{LoRA}}\cdot\|\Delta\theta_{k}\|\leq m (additive, O⁡(d)O(d)) rather than the exponentially large product Lfull=∏k(1+Lk)L_{\text{full}}=\prod_{k}(1+L_{k}).

Full derivation in Appendix A.7.

C.6 Hölder–Jensen Approximation

For practical deployment over NN steps with risk budget B=∑δnB=\sum\delta_{n}, applying the per-step Hölder bound and Jensen’s inequality yields:

Umax​(N,B)=Cα⋅N1−β⋅BβU_{\max}(N,B)=C_{\alpha}\cdot N^{1-\beta}\cdot B^{\beta}

with optimal uniform allocation δn=B/N\delta_{n}=B/N. This bound is looser than the exact NP-based ceiling U∗​(N,B)=N⋅TPRNP​(B/N)U^{*}(N,B)=N\cdot\mathrm{TPR}_{\mathrm{NP}}(B/N) (Theorem 5), which is 1.4–3.1×\times tighter at N=102N=10^{2}–10610^{6}.

C.7 Multi-Dimensional Tradeoff Surface

Classifiers occupy: TPR≤Cα⋅δβ\mathrm{TPR}\leq C_{\alpha}\cdot\delta^{\beta}, 𝒞=O⁡(d2)\mathcal{C}=O(d^{2}), n=Ω⁡(dVC/δ2)n=\Omega(d_{\text{VC}}/\delta^{2}).

Verifiers occupy: δ=0\delta=0, TPR>0\mathrm{TPR}>0 (domain-restricted), 𝒞=O⁡(d)\mathcal{C}=O(d), n=0n=0.

These regions are disconnected on the δ=0\delta=0 hyperplane.

D.2 Information-Theoretic Bound Comparison

The Hölder bound is tighter per-step for small δ\delta; the MI bound is complementary for cumulative analysis. Both bounds are valid across all distributions tested.

D.3 Sample Complexity Simulation

Simulated logistic regression (dVC=11d_{\text{VC}}=11, Δs=0.5\Delta_{s}=0.5, k=5k=5): 200/200 steps sample-starved; ∑δ=41.17\sum\delta=41.17 (diverges). Confirms Proposition 2.

D.5 Pareto Frontier Visualization

The classifier and verifier regions are disconnected on the δ=0\delta=0 hyperplane. Classifiers require Ω⁡(dVC/δ2)\Omega(d_{\text{VC}}/\delta^{2}) samples and cannot reach δ=0\delta=0 with TPR>0\mathrm{TPR}>0. The ball verifier operates at δ=0\delta=0 with no training data.

D.6 Trained Classifier Ceiling

Across all 72 (classifier, δ\delta) pairs tested (4 classifiers ×\times 6 δ\delta values ×\times 3 separations), zero violations of the Hölder bound were observed. Trained classifiers achieve TPR ratios of 0.52–0.94 relative to the Hölder ceiling.

D.7 Non-Gaussian Tightness Validation

Across 8 non-Gaussian families (Laplace, Student-tt, Gaussian mixture): min ratios 0.28–0.40, average ratios 0.54–0.70. The bound is uniformly valid and tight across heavy-tailed and multi-modal distributions.

D.8 Lipschitz Ball Verifier Demonstration

LTC controller (d=240d=240), L=13.75L=13.75, r=0.0208r=0.0208. Inside-ball: 200/200 safe (δ=0\delta=0), TPR=0.286\mathrm{TPR}=0.286.

D.9 NP Counting Proof Validation

All 9 configs satisfy direct sum ≤\leq counting bound (ratios 0.33–0.89). Counting 13% tighter than Hölder at Δs=1.0,p=2.0\Delta_{s}=1.0,p=2.0.

D.10 Tight Finite-Horizon Validation

The exact ceiling grows subpolynomially: from N=104N=10^{4} to N=106N=10^{6} (100×\times increase in NN), U∗U^{*} grows only 2.66×\times. Uniform allocation optimal (Jensen). MI bound is loose by 4–86×\times.

Appendix E Computational Complexity and Open Problems

E.1 Connection to Computational Complexity

The information-theoretic bound (Proposition 1) and sample complexity barrier (Proposition 2) connect to a broader question: is safe self-improvement computationally hard? A natural extension is whether satisfying the dual conditions is NP-hard.

E.2 Open Problems

  1. 1.

    Computational impossibility. Is satisfying the dual conditions NP-hard, beyond being statistically impossible?

  2. 2.

    Adaptive verification. Can tighter verified regions (e.g., ellipsoidal) maintain O⁡(d)O(d) checking? Ball chaining experiments in [23] provide an initial empirical answer.

  3. 3.

    Multi-agent and continuous-time extensions of the dual conditions.
